01 · The problem and our solution

When something feels wrong far from Earth, the crew can’t wait for a doctor. Void Voyagers turns one reading into one verdict and one next step, with no signal needed.

A check takesAbout 1 minute
The verdictNominal to Urgent
Needs a connectionNever

Public benefit

Why it matters on Earth

Far from Earth or far from a clinic, the need is the same: know what a reading means and what to do now. The same offline, private checks could serve polar crews, sailors and remote communities, with no account and no cost.

How to use it

03 · 4 steps
  1. Pick your mission

    Station, Moon, Mars transit or Mars base, at the top.

  2. Do today’s checks

    Each has step-by-step instructions on Today.

  3. Read the verdict

    Nominal, Watch, Act or Urgent, plus the next step.

  4. Look it up or report

    Library for answers; send the flight surgeon a report you’ve read first.

The console starts with a made-up 42-day mission. Press “Start my own log” there to use your own. After the first visit everything works offline, and you can install it as an app from the browser menu.

        Your private space

        Mind is not therapy and not a medical record. Your journal, letters and team check-ins are encrypted with your passphrase and never sent anywhere. Mood ratings, wellbeing answers and the names and dates you add are stored like your other readings: only on this device, protected by its lock screen, not by the passphrase. Reports leave out your mood and wellbeing answers unless you tick them yourself. If things feel heavy, you don’t have to carry it alone: talk to your crew medical officer or your behavioural health team.

        How it works

        Guide

        Plain-language help for checking yourself in space. No medical training assumed.

        Four colours, four actions

        Nominal

        Inside the healthy range for you and this mission. Keep your routine.

        Watch

        A little outside your normal. Look after yourself, re-check, and mention it at your next private medical conference.

        Act

        Needs attention today. Follow the steps shown and tell your crew medical officer.

        Urgent

        Possible emergency. Alert your crewmates, start the onboard emergency procedure and contact the flight surgeon on the priority channel.

        Every status has a shape and a word as well as a colour, so it reads the same on any screen, in any light, and with colour-blindness.

        When to call for help

        1. Look after yourself

          Sleep, eat your full ration, drink to your target and do your exercise. Most problems in space start small.

        2. Re-check, then mention it

          Repeat the measurement the right way (see How to measure). If it stays outside your normal, raise it at your weekly private medical conference with the flight surgeon.

        3. Tell your crew medical officer today

          On the ISS each crew has two crew medical officers (CMOs). They are usually not doctors, but they are trained to examine you, use the onboard medical kit and bring in the flight surgeon.

        4. Emergency: act now

          Alert your crewmates and start the onboard procedure first. Near Earth the flight surgeon is on call 24 hours a day. From Mars a message takes 3–22 minutes each way and there is no early ride home, so the crew must act before help can answer.

        Why check yourself in space?

        Your body changes quickly. In weightlessness about 2 litres of fluid shift towards your head, blood plasma falls by roughly 10–15%, weight-bearing bone lost 1–1.5% a month even with the exercise devices of Mir and the early ISS (about 0.5–1% with today’s), and most crew sleep only about 6 hours a night. Catching a change early turns a mission-ending problem into a small fix.

        Help is far away. From the space station, Earth is about a day away. From the Moon it is several days; from Mars there is no early return at all. The further you go, the more your crew has to notice, judge and treat on its own. That is what Void Voyagers is for.

        What you can measure yourself: heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, temperature, a finger-stick glucose, sleep, mood, a 3-minute reaction test, near vision and the Amsler grid, fluids, exercise and body mass, plus cabin CO₂ and your radiation dosimeter. Bone density, eye scans and blood chemistry need specialist equipment and the medical team.

        How Void Voyagers decides. Each reading is compared with clinical early-warning ranges (NEWS2, AHA/ACC 2025, ADA 2026, sleep-medicine consensus) and NASA limits. Where no fixed number exists, it compares the reading with your own baseline. Rules that are Void Voyagers design choices, such as the reaction-test band, are marked in How to measure.

        The five hazards of spaceflight

        NASA groups the dangers of spaceflight into five hazards. Each one shows up in the measurements you take.

        Why bones weaken in space, and what helps

        What happens

        Without gravity your bones carry no load. Cells that remove bone speed up while bone-building cells lag. Hip and spine lose about 1–1.5% a month, roughly what an older adult loses in a year.

        Load it heavy

        Heavy resistance exercise (squats, deadlifts and heel raises at 100% of body weight or more) plus treadmill running protects most sites. ISS crews exercise about 2 hours a day, 6 days a week.

        Fuel it

        Eat your full ration with enough protein and vitamin D, and keep sodium at 2,300 mg a day or less (NASA’s exploration requirement is 1,500–2,300 mg). Weight loss and salty food both speed up bone loss.

        Protect your kidneys

        Calcium from bone ends up in urine and can form stones. Drink to your fluid target. Flank pain with blood in urine means contacting the flight surgeon now.

        Medication

        Exercise alone does not stop loss of the hip’s spongy inner bone. In an ISS study, exercise plus weekly alendronate attenuated loss at the spine, hip and pelvis, and NASA experts have suggested a pre-flight zoledronic acid infusion for missions of a year or more. Only the flight surgeon can prescribe them.

        After landing

        Recovery is slow and often incomplete: 9 of 17 astronauts had not regained shin density a year after landing. Keep loading, follow the walking-to-jogging plan and attend your follow-up scans.

        The bone estimate (Today → Bones & muscles) comes from the team’s Orbit Health bone module. Sources: NASA HRP bone fracture evidence report (2024); LeBlanc 2013; Smith 2012; Sibonga 2019; Vico 2017; Gabel 2022; Stavnichuk 2020; Lane 2013.

        Mission environments

        The ISS rate is effective dose. The Moon, transit and Mars rates are dose equivalent measured behind light shielding (China’s Chang’e-4 lander and NASA’s Curiosity rover), so they run high for a shielded habitat; NASA’s design ceilings are 1.3 mSv/day in free space and 0.9 on a surface. Your dosimeter shows absorbed dose in mGy, so the app compares it with absorbed-dose baselines, never with the mSv figures.

        From ESA’s Space Heritage archive

        1981 · ESTEC-PHOTO-1981.10.157

        Sled training for Spacelab-1

        ESA astronauts Ulf Merbold and Wubbo Ockels trained on the sled used to study balance and space sickness in weightlessness. About 70% of crew still feel space-sick for the first 2–3 days.

        1984 · ESTEC-PHOTO-1984.12.009

        Astronaut sleep restraint

        A sleep restraint designed and demonstrated by ESA astronaut Wubbo Ockels. Sleeping well in space is still hard: crews average about 6 hours a night.

        1984 · ESA BR-17

        A Survey of Space Biology and Space Medicine

        ESA’s early overview of how weightlessness affects the heart, balance organs and skeleton: the same systems Void Voyagers tracks today.

        Void Voyagers is a training and research prototype built by team Void Voyagers for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It is not a medical device and does not replace your crew medical officer, flight surgeon or doctor.

        Knowledge base

        Library

        Plain-language notes on the health problems crews meet most often in space, and on the medicines a flight kit carries. Every entry lists the sources it comes from. How the app decides is in the Guide.

        Show

        Doses are worked out from your latest readings. Void Voyagers uses the official label dose, never goes above the label maximum, and stops you when a reading makes a medicine unsafe. Medicines given by a medic show the label dose only. Always confirm with your crew medical officer or the onboard checklist before taking anything.

        If this is happening now: alert your crewmates, start the onboard emergency procedure and call the flight surgeon on the priority channel. Don’t wait to read on.

        For learning and training only. The Library does not diagnose anything. If a reading or a symptom worries you, follow the steps on Today and talk to your crew medical officer.

        Last updated 15 November 2026

        Privacy charter

        Our six commitments to every crew member:

        1. Your health data stays on this device unless you choose to send a report.
        2. Nothing leaves without your tap. Apart from loading the page itself, only three buttons send anything, and each says what it sends.
        3. No accounts, cookies, analytics, advertising or trackers.
        4. You see every report before it is sent. Only the team can read the inbox, and every report is deleted automatically after 90 days.
        5. You can download or delete everything at any time in Crew profile & data.
        6. Open and auditable. The full source code is public on GitHub under the MIT license.

        Who is responsible

        Team Void Voyagers, the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026 team that built this app, is responsible for the report inbox (the “data controller”). To ask about your data or have a report deleted, write to us privately through the private report form on our GitHub page, with the time you sent the report and your callsign. Nobody else can see that message.

        What Void Voyagers stores, and where

        • Your readings, crew profile (pre-flight mass, sex for the fluid target, mission dates, bone medication plan), the symptoms you tick, emergency and storm-shelter logs, your medicine-kit list, reports waiting to be sent, and settings (including the place you chose for Window to Earth and your body-map view) are saved in this browser’s local storage under the keys voidvoyagers.v1 and voidvoyagers.theme. They never leave the device unless you send a report.
        • To work without a connection, Void Voyagers keeps a copy of the app itself (its page, fonts and 3D model, never your data) in the browser’s cache.
        • Anyone who uses this browser on this device can open Void Voyagers and see your readings. On a shared device, delete your data when you finish.
        • Backups you download are ordinary files you keep. They are not encrypted, so anyone with the file can read your readings: store it somewhere safe.
        • If you open Void Voyagers as a file saved on a computer rather than as the website, other web pages saved on that computer can read its storage. For private use, open the website (it keeps working offline after the first visit).
        • “Delete all my data” in Crew profile & data removes everything listed above from this device.

        No cookies

        Void Voyagers does not set or read cookies, and it uses no third-party scripts, fonts or trackers: its fonts, 3D viewer and model are served from the same site as the app.

        When something leaves your device

        Only when you press a button that says so:

        • Window to Earth (“Show latest view”) sends the place you chose (its coordinates) to Microsoft’s Planetary Computer to find a recent satellite image from NASA’s HLS data. No health data is sent. If you use your own coordinates, pick a place you are happy to share rather than your home.
        • Space weather (“Check space weather”) asks NASA’s DONKI service at api.nasa.gov for solar events in the last 30 days. Only a date range and the app’s public demo key are sent, with no health data.
        • Send report to flight surgeon sends the report you are shown first: your latest reading of each check with its time and age, the findings and advice (which can include your wellbeing and mood answers), symptoms you ticked in the last 24 hours, the emergency log if there is one, your mission environment and day, your pre-flight body mass and bone medication plan, whether it is example data, and an optional callsign (please don’t use your real name). It goes to the team’s inbox, a Supabase database in the EU (Frankfurt). With no connection, the report waits on this device and is sent when the connection returns.

        All of these requests are made with cookies switched off and without a referrer. Like any web request, each service sees your IP address and browser type, and keeps it briefly under its own privacy policy. Microsoft and NASA are US organisations. Links to other sites, such as NASA, GitHub and journals, open those sites, where their own privacy policies and cookies apply.

        The report inbox

        In this prototype the Void Voyagers team reads the inbox. It is not a real flight surgeon, it is not watched around the clock, and nobody will reply with medical advice. If you need help now, contact your crew medical officer, your doctor or local emergency services. Don’t wait for a report.

        The public key in the app can only add reports, at most 30 a minute across the inbox; nobody can read them back through it. Reports are deleted automatically 90 days after they arrive.

        Why we may use a report, and your rights

        We use a report only because you chose to send it: pressing “Send report” is your explicit consent. You can withdraw it at any time by asking us to delete the report. You can also ask for a copy, ask us to correct it, or object to how we use it, through the private report form above, and you can complain to your data protection authority.

        Children

        Void Voyagers is not meant for children. If you are under 16, use the checks on your device but don’t send a report. If we learn that a report came from a child, we delete it.

        Hosting

        The website is served by Vercel and Microsoft Azure. GitHub hosts only the source code and the research document. Like any web server, these providers log technical data such as your IP address and browser type to deliver the page and protect against abuse, and keep it for a short time under their own privacy policies. We don’t use these logs to identify or track anyone. Vercel and Microsoft are US companies and may process this data outside the EU under their data processing terms.

        Not a medical device

        Void Voyagers is a research and training prototype built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026. It does not replace your crew medical officer, flight surgeon or doctor. Do not rely on it for real medical decisions.

        Contact

        Private questions and deletion requests: the private report form. General questions: open an issue on the project’s GitHub page.
